sections.normalized_html:
We need to show that

  • if [MATH: p^m \mid q^n] then [MATH: p = q,] and

  • if [MATH: q^n \mid p^m] then [MATH: p = q.]

Let's suppose [MATH: p^m \mid q^n.] For a contradiction, let's assume [MATH: p \neq q.] Then, [MATH: \textrm{gcd}(p,q) = 1,] and there exist integers [MATH: r] and [MATH: s] such that [MATH: pr + qs = 1.] Since [MATH: p \mid p^m] and [MATH: p^m \mid q^n,] by the transitivity of division, [MATH: p \mid q^n.] Now, multiplying the above equation by [MATH: q^{n-1},] we get [MATH: prq^{n-1} + q^n s = q^{n-1}]

Looking at the left-hand side of this equation, we have that

  • [MATH: p \mid prq^{n-1}] (since it has a factor [MATH: p]), and

  • [MATH: p \mid q^n s] (since [MATH: p \mid q^n,] as we deduced earlier).

Hence, [MATH: p \mid q^{n-1}.]

Repeating the same argument several times, we obtain that [MATH: p \mid q^{n}, \quad p \mid q^{n-1}, \quad p \mid q^{n-2}, \quad p \mid q^{n-3}, \quad \ldots,] and, eventually, [MATH: p \mid q.] But this is a contradiction because [MATH: p] and [MATH: q] are distinct primes.

Therefore, our assumption that [MATH: p \neq q] was wrong. Therefore, [MATH: p=q.]

Content:
In this lesson, we'll focus on understanding and applying divisibility properties with prime numbers.

Content:
Let's state our first property:

Content:
Theorem

Content:

>
> [MATH: \qquad] [MATH: p^m \mid q^n \quad\textrm{or}\quad q^n \mid p^m \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad p = q.]

Content:
We can prove this property using proof by contradiction.

Content:
Proof

Content:
> We need to show that
>
> - if [MATH: p^m \mid q^n] then [MATH: p = q,] and
> - if [MATH: q^n \mid p^m] then [MATH: p = q.]
>
> Let's suppose [MATH: p^m \mid q^n.] For a contradiction, let's assume [MATH: p \neq q.] Then, [MATH: \textrm{gcd}(p,q) = 1,] and there exist integers [MATH: r] and [MATH: s] such that
> [MATH: pr + qs = 1.]
> Since [MATH: p \mid p^m] and [MATH: p^m \mid q^n,] by the transitivity of division, [MATH: p \mid q^n.] Now, multiplying the above equation by [MATH: q^{n-1},] we get
> [MATH: prq^{n-1} + q^n s = q^{n-1}]
>
> Looking at the left-hand side of this equation, we have that
>
> - [MATH: p \mid prq^{n-1}] (since it has a factor [MATH: p]), and
> - [MATH: p \mid q^n s] (since [MATH: p \mid q^n,] as we deduced earlier).
>
> Hence, [MATH: p \mid q^{n-1}.]
>

> [MATH: p \mid q^{n}, \quad p \mid q^{n-1}, \quad p \mid q^{n-2}, \quad p \mid q^{n-3}, \quad \ldots,]
> and, eventually, [MATH: p \mid q.] But this is a contradiction because [MATH: p] and [MATH: q] are distinct primes.

Theorem (Euclid's Lemma)

Content:
> For any integers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] and any prime [MATH: p,]
>
> [MATH: \qquad] [MATH: p \:|\: ab] [MATH: \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad] [MATH: p \:|\: a \quad] or [MATH: \quad p \:|\: b.]

Content:
So, if [MATH: p] divides a product of two factors, then [MATH: p] divides at least one of the factors.

Content:
Proof

> [MATH: pr + as = \textrm{gcd}(a,p)=1.]
> On the other hand, given that [MATH: p\: | \: ab,] there exists an integer [MATH: k] such that
> [MATH: ab=pk.]
> Multiplying both sides of the first equation by [MATH: b] and substituting [MATH: ab=pk,] we obtain the following:
> [MATH: pr + as|= 1; (pr + as)b|= b; prb + (ab)s|= b; prb + (pk)s|= b; p(rb + ks)|= b.]
> Since [MATH: r,b,k,] and [MATH: s] are integers, then [MATH: rb + ks] is an integer too. Hence,
> [MATH: p\: | \: b.]
> Similarly, if we assume that [MATH: p] does not divide [MATH: b,] we get that [MATH: p \: | \: a.]

Recall that for any integers [MATH: a,] [MATH: b,] and [MATH: c,]

[MATH: c \:|\: ab \quad] and [MATH: \quad \text{gcd}(a,c)=1] [MATH: \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad] [MATH: \quad c \:|\: b.]

Also, given that [MATH: p] and [MATH: q] are primes, we get

[MATH: p^m \:|\: q^n] [MATH: \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad] [MATH: p = q,]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll focus on understanding and applying divisibility properties with prime numbers.

Content:
Let's state our first property:

Content:
Theorem

Content:
> For any positive integers [MATH: m] and [MATH: n] and any prime numbers [MATH: p] and [MATH: q,] we have that
>
> [MATH: \qquad] [MATH: p^m \mid q^n \quad\textrm{or}\quad q^n \mid p^m \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad p = q.]

Content:
We can prove this property using proof by contradiction.

Content:
Proof

Content:
> We need to show that
>
> - if [MATH: p^m \mid q^n] then [MATH: p = q,] and
> - if [MATH: q^n \mid p^m] then [MATH: p = q.]
>
> Let's suppose [MATH: p^m \mid q^n.] For a contradiction, let's assume [MATH: p \neq q.] Then, [MATH: \textrm{gcd}(p,q) = 1,] and there exist integers [MATH: r] and [MATH: s] such that
> [MATH: pr + qs = 1.]
> Since [MATH: p \mid p^m] and [MATH: p^m \mid q^n,] by the transitivity of division, [MATH: p \mid q^n.] Now, multiplying the above equation by [MATH: q^{n-1},] we get
> [MATH: prq^{n-1} + q^n s = q^{n-1}]
>
> Looking at the left-hand side of this equation, we have that
>
> - [MATH: p \mid prq^{n-1}] (since it has a factor [MATH: p]), and
> - [MATH: p \mid q^n s] (since [MATH: p \mid q^n,] as we deduced earlier).
>
> Hence, [MATH: p \mid q^{n-1}.]
>
> Repeating the same argument several times, we obtain that
> [MATH: p \mid q^{n}, \quad p \mid q^{n-1}, \quad p \mid q^{n-2}, \quad p \mid q^{n-3}, \quad \ldots,]
> and, eventually, [MATH: p \mid q.] But this is a contradiction because [MATH: p] and [MATH: q] are distinct primes.
>
> Therefore, our assumption that [MATH: p \neq q] was wrong. Therefore, [MATH: p=q.]

Content:
Note that the case [MATH: q^n \mid p^m\Rightarrow q\mid p] is proved in the same way.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying True Statements Concerning Prime Divisibility

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: q] be a prime number. Which of the following statements are true?

1. If [MATH: 9\: | \ q^5] then [MATH: q = 3]
2. If [MATH: q^2 \: | \: 2^3] then [MATH: q = 8]
3. If [MATH: q^2 \: | \: 8] then [MATH: q = 2]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For any integers [MATH: m] and [MATH: n] and any prime numbers [MATH: p] and [MATH: q,] we have that

> [MATH: p^m \mid q^n \quad\textrm{or}\quad q^n \mid p^m
> \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad p = q.]

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements.

- Statement I is true. Since [MATH: 9=3^2] and [MATH: 9 \: | \: q^5,] then [MATH: 3^2 \: | \: q^5.] As [MATH: 3] and [MATH: q] are prime numbers, [MATH: 2] and [MATH: 5] are integers, and [MATH: 3^2\: | \ q^5,] we must have [MATH: q = 3.]
- Statement II is false. As a counterexample, let [MATH: {\color{blue}{q}}={\color{blue}{2}}.] Then, [MATH: {\color{blue}{2}}^2\mid 2^3] but [MATH: {\color{blue}{2}}\neq 8.]
- Statement III is true. Since [MATH: 8=2^3] and [MATH: q^2 \: | \: 8,] then [MATH: q^2 \: | \: 2^3.] As [MATH: q] and [MATH: 2] are prime numbers, [MATH: 2] and [MATH: 3] are integers, and [MATH: q^2\: | \ 2^3,] we must have [MATH: q = 2.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

Item 5 — Tutorial: Euclid's Lemma

Content:
Let's state our next property, often called Euclid's lemma.

Content:
Theorem (Euclid's Lemma)

Content:
> For any integers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] and any prime [MATH: p,]
>
> [MATH: \qquad] [MATH: p \:|\: ab] [MATH: \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad] [MATH: p \:|\: a \quad] or [MATH: \quad p \:|\: b.]

Content:
So, if [MATH: p] divides a product of two factors, then [MATH: p] divides at least one of the factors.

Content:
Proof

Content:
> Suppose that [MATH: p] does not divide [MATH: a.] We must show that [MATH: p] divides [MATH: b.]
>
> If the prime [MATH: p] does not divide [MATH: a,] then [MATH: p] is not a factor in the prime decomposition of [MATH: a.] Therefore, [MATH: a] and [MATH: p] must be coprime. This means there exist integers [MATH: r] and [MATH: s] such that
> [MATH: pr + as = \textrm{gcd}(a,p)=1.]
> On the other hand, given that [MATH: p\: | \: ab,] there exists an integer [MATH: k] such that
> [MATH: ab=pk.]
> Multiplying both sides of the first equation by [MATH: b] and substituting [MATH: ab=pk,] we obtain the following:
> [MATH: pr + as|= 1; (pr + as)b|= b; prb + (ab)s|= b; prb + (pk)s|= b; p(rb + ks)|= b.]
> Since [MATH: r,b,k,] and [MATH: s] are integers, then [MATH: rb + ks] is an integer too. Hence,
> [MATH: p\: | \: b.]
> Similarly, if we assume that [MATH: p] does not divide [MATH: b,] we get that [MATH: p \: | \: a.]

- Statement II is false. As a counterexample, let [MATH: {\color{blue}{a}}={\color{blue}{1}}.] Then, [MATH: 7\mid 14\cdot {\color{blue}{1}}] but [MATH: 7\not\mid {\color{blue}{1}}.]
